## Data Acquisition


``` {r}
#| output: false

#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

```{r}

library(dplyr)

top_ten <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1") |> 
  slice_max(order_by=Views, n=10) |> select(Title, hours_viewed)

sum_top_ten <- top_ten |> select(hours_viewed) |> sum()

```
`{r} watch_time_percent` of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1.
I interpreted Top 10 titles to mean the top ten most viewed, so for this, I created a filter for just 2026H1 content, then sorted the views. Then I had to find the **TOTAL** watch time of all content from 2023H1 to 2026H1.

Finally I used the total watch time of Top 10 title of 2026H1 and divided that by the total watch time of all of the content.

#1
``` {r}

library(gt)


total_views <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(sum(Views, na.rm = TRUE))
#total_views

# top show by total viewed in each period
NETFLIX_DATA |> select(Title, period, Views) |> drop_na() |>
  group_by(period) |> slice_max(Views) |>
  # fraction of total views it captured
  mutate((Views/total_views)) |> 
  rename(fraction_total_views = `sum(Views, na.rm = TRUE)`) |>
  mutate(Views=comma(Views),
         fraction_total_views=percent(fraction_total_views,accuracy=.0001)) |>
  ungroup() |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Top Shows (by Total Viewership)", 
             subtitle="Top shows in each period and the fraction of total viewership they captured") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="calculated by dividing each period's 
               views by the total views of the dataset (60,089,800,000)",
               locations=cells_column_labels(columns = fraction_total_views))


# total hours viewed
tot_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(sum(hours_viewed))
#tot_hours

# top show by total hours viewed in each period
NETFLIX_DATA |> select(Title,period, hours_viewed) |>
  group_by(period) |> 
  slice_max(hours_viewed) |>
  # fraction of total views it captured
  mutate((hours_viewed/tot_hours)) |> 
  rename(fraction_total_hrs_views = `sum(hours_viewed)`) |>
  mutate(hours_viewed=comma(hours_viewed),
         fraction_total_hrs_views=percent(fraction_total_hrs_views,accuracy=.0001)) |>
  rename(`Hours Viewed` = hours_viewed, 
         `Fraction of Total Hours Viewed` = fraction_total_hrs_views) |>
  ungroup() |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="top shows (by total hours viewed)", 
             subtitle="top shows in each period and the fraction of total viewership they captured") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="calculated by dividing each period's 
               hours_viewed by the total hours_viewed of the dataset (511,590,500,000)",
               locations=cells_column_labels(columns = `Fraction of Total Hours Viewed`))

```
The first table is the top shows in each period by views and the fraction of total viewership it captured.
The 2023H1 dataset didn't have a Views column, so the tables I've generated will only reflect 2023H2 to 2026H1. 

I also made another table using hours_viewed as the metric instead, to see if there was a significant difference and I thought it would be nice to include 2023H1 to analyze. 

In my opinion, hours_viewed may be more informative than total views because Views seems to act more like a click counter, while hours_viewed takes into account content that are dropped as it shows how long people sit through the show/movie.



#2 
```{r}

#2 How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? 
#You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.

# number of title
NETFLIX_DATA |> select(period,Title) |> 
  group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(total_titles = n() |> comma()) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Number of Titles by Period")
 
# total content runtime
NETFLIX_DATA |> select(period,Title,Runtime) |> 
  group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(total_runtime = sum(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)|> comma())  |> 
  gt() |> tab_header(title="Total Content Runtime by Period")


```
The first table is the Number of Title by period and the second is total content runtime by period. Content runtime is increasing while the number of titles by period is decreasing. There is a huge drop in number of titles from 2023H1 to 2023H2 so I'm guessing that Netflix either revamped their data reporting in between those two periods, dropped content, or lost streaming rights to licensed content. Since 2023H2, number of titles has been increasing by small amounts each period.

The increase in content runtime may be a result of the increase in number of content. 2023H1 is anomalous in that the number of titles is over twice as large as 2023H2, but content runtime is **lower** that 2023H2.



# 3
```{r}

#3 Which shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? 
#These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back ... e.g., re-runs of Friends.

# compute the average viewership, the minimum viewership, 
#and the standard deviation of viewership across different periods 
#and develop a filter using some combination of these quantities.

# period_stats a table of the statistics (mean, standard deviation, and min views) of each period
period_stats <- NETFLIX_DATA |> group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(period_mean = mean(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE), 
            period_sd=sd(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE),
            period_min=min(as.numeric(Views), na.rm=TRUE))
period_stats

get(period_min)

  # shows_higher_than_avg are the shows with viewship higher than that period's average
shows_higher_than_avg <- inner_join(period_stats, NETFLIX_DATA, join_by(period == period)) |> 
  filter_out(is.na(Views)) |>  
  select(period, Title, period_mean, Views) |>
  filter((Views > period_mean)) |> 
  mutate(Views=comma(Views), period_mean=comma(period_mean)) |> gt() |>
  tab_header(title="Higher Than Average Shows") |>
  tab_options(
    container.height = px(300),
    container.overflow.y = TRUE 
  )
shows_higher_than_avg

# stdev_multiplier - adjust the number of standard deviations to move away from mean
stdev_multiplier <- 6
period_standard_devs <- period_stats |> select(period, period_mean, period_sd) |> 
  mutate(stdev_multiplied = period_mean + (stdev_multiplier * period_sd))
#period_standard_devs

# shows with viewership greather than the period's average + multiplier * the period's stdev
# default sorted by period.
inner_join(period_standard_devs, NETFLIX_DATA, join_by(period == period)) |> 
  filter_out(is.na(Views)) |> mutate(mean_plus_stdev_multiplied = period_mean+stdev_multiplied) |> 
  select(period, Title, Views, period_mean, stdev_multiplied, mean_plus_stdev_multiplied) |> 
  filter((Views > stdev_multiplied)) |>
  mutate(Views=comma(Views), 
         period_mean=comma(period_mean),
         stdev_multiplied=comma(stdev_multiplied), 
         mean_plus_stdev_multiplied=comma(mean_plus_stdev_multiplied)) |>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Views > Mean + (Multiplier * Standard Deviation)",
             subtitle="shows with viewership greater than the period's average + multiplier * the period's stdev") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="This is the number that each title's View count is being compared to. 
               This number varies between periods. 
               It's the sum of the period's standard deviation times 6, and the period's mean.",
               locations = cells_column_labels(columns = mean_plus_stdev_multiplied)) |>
  tab_options(
    container.height = px(300), 
    container.overflow.y = TRUE  
  )


```
The 3rd and 4th tables are the list of shows with the most consistently high viewership across all periods. 

The minimum View is the same across all of the periods, so I'm assuming that Netflix only tracks and records content that have at least that many views. And since the minimum is the same across all periods, I didn't use minimum for this analysis. Instead, I focused on the mean and standard deviations.

In addition to using the standard deviation, I created a variable called stdev_multiplier, which is used to adjust the number of standard deviations to move away from mean. I wanted to capture the titles with the **HIGHEST** views, so I used the mean (of each period) and added the standard deviation (of the corresponding period) to try to capture the top 13 percentile? https://lesn.appstate.edu/olson/normal_curve.htm
I kept increasing the percentiles to narrow the amount of titles further by using a constant (which I called *multiplier*): (mean + (multiplier*standard deviation))
I settled on a constant (or multiplier) of 6 --> ((6 x standard deviation of each period) + mean)
I am comparing the views of each show to its period's mean+(std_constant*std dev) to get the top top top tier content

The results are surprising because I expected to see Friends or Seinfeld, while there are other content here that I was not expecting to see. It's possible I did something wrong but the presence of Stranger Things, Squid Games, and Bridgerton slightly assuages my fears. In fact, some seasons of these shows appear on the list more than once, in a different period, so I don't think the numbers I got were too far. 





```{r}
#4 Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?
#hours viewed of shows / total hours viewed

#Length: anything over 4-ish hours is almost certainly a TV show, not a movie
#“Season”: if a title has “Season” in it, it is almost certainly a TV show

# total hours viewed of all content
total_hours_viewed <- NETFLIX_DATA |> summarize(sum(hours_viewed))
#total_hours_viewed

# 4 hours = 240 minutes
# filters:
# these filter out possible shows: content with < 240min runtime, or title contains "season"
shows <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(Runtime >= 240 | str_detect(Title, "Season")) |> 
  group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(shows_hours_viewed=sum(hours_viewed)) |> mutate(total_hours_viewed) 
shows |> 
  mutate(shows_hours_viewed = comma(shows_hours_viewed)) |> 
  select(-`sum(hours_viewed)`)|>
  gt() |> tab_header(title="Total Hours Viewed for Shows, by Period")

movies <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(Runtime < 240 & Runtime > 75) |> group_by(period) |> 
  summarize(movies_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed)) |> mutate(total_hours_viewed)
movies |> 
  mutate(movies_hours_viewed = comma(movies_hours_viewed)) |> 
  select(-`sum(hours_viewed)`) |>
  gt()|> tab_header(title="Total Hours Viewed for Movies, by Period")


#what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?
shows |> mutate(shows_fraction = shows_hours_viewed / `sum(hours_viewed)`) |> 
  select(-`sum(hours_viewed)`) |> 
  mutate(shows_hours_viewed = comma(shows_hours_viewed)) |> 
  mutate(shows_fraction = percent(shows_fraction, accuracy=.01)) |>
  gt() |> tab_header(title="Fraction of Time Spent on Shows") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="shows_fraction was calculated by hours viewed of shows / total hours viewed") 
movies |> mutate(movies_fraction = movies_hours_viewed / `sum(hours_viewed)`) |> 
  select(-`sum(hours_viewed)`) |> 
  mutate(movies_hours_viewed = comma(movies_hours_viewed)) |> 
  mutate(movies_fraction = percent(movies_fraction, accuracy=.01)) |>
  gt() |>  tab_header(title="Fraction of Time Spent on Movies") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="movies_fraction was calculated by hours viewed of movies / total hours viewed")


##### for corporate strategy memo 
total_hours <- inner_join(shows, movies, join_by(period)) |> 
  mutate(tot = shows_hours_viewed + movies_hours_viewed ) |> 
  select(-`sum(hours_viewed).x`, -`sum(hours_viewed).y`)
total_hours |> 
  mutate(tot = comma(tot)) |> 
  rename(total = tot) |>
  gt()

#####


```
Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?

Tables 3 and 4 show the fraction of time spent on shows vs movies by period. There is a possibility that not all content were captured in the filter I had used to differentiate shows from movies: content with more than 240 minute runtime, or titles containing "season" are shows, content with Runtime > 75 and < 240 are movies. Overall, the fraction of time spent on shows is higher than on movies across all periods.






#5
```{r}

# 5 How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? 

#Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? 
# Percent difference = (avg live − avg taped) ÷ avg taped × 100

# means of live content
live_ <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(live_event == TRUE) |> 
  summarize(live_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))

#mean of taped content
taped_ <- NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(live_event == FALSE) |> 
  summarize(taped_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))


# live average views, taped average views, percent diff
live_|> mutate(taped_) |>
  mutate(percent_diff = (live_mean - taped_) / taped_ ) |> 
  mutate(taped_mean = comma(taped_mean), 
         live_mean=comma(live_mean),
         live_percent_difference=percent(percent_diff$taped_mean,accuracy=.01)) |>
  select(-percent_diff)|>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title="Percent Difference of Live vs Taped Content, by Views") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="")




#How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?
#Does a ‘top tier’ live event draw more viewership than a ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?

# average viewership of live top tier content

#top tier mean of live content
live_top_tier <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(live_event == TRUE) |> drop_na() |>
  select(Title, Views) |> 
  mutate(live_) |>
  filter(Views > live_mean) |> #print(n=96) |>
  summarize(live_top_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))
#live_top_tier 

# top tier mean of taped content
taped_top_tier <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(live_event == FALSE) |> drop_na() |>
  select(Title, Views) |>
  mutate(taped_) |> 
  filter(Views > taped_mean) |> 
  summarize(taped_top_mean = mean(Views,na.rm=TRUE))
#taped_top_tier

# percent difference of top tier content
live_top_tier|> mutate(taped_top_tier) |>
  mutate(top_tier_percent_diff = (live_top_mean - taped_top_tier) / taped_top_tier ) |>
  mutate(taped_top_mean = comma(taped_top_mean), 
         live_top_mean = comma(live_top_mean),
         top_tier_percent_difference = percent(top_tier_percent_diff$taped_top_mean,accuracy=.01))|>
  select(-top_tier_percent_diff)|>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Top Tier Live vs Pre-taped Content, by Views") |>
  tab_footnote(footnote="")


# higher than average LIVE content
NETFLIX_DATA |> 
  filter(live_event == TRUE) |> 
  arrange(desc(Views)) |> 
  select(Title, Views, live_event) |>
  mutate(Views = comma(Views)) |>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(title="Top Tier Live Content (by Views)")


```
The average live event drew slightly more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped, if judging by percent difference of average live content vs average taped content. [Percent difference = (average live − average taped) ÷ average taped × 100]

Taking the mean of live content and comparing that to the mean of taped content, the percent difference is `{r}live_percent_difference` higher views for live content. I found this surprising because there was not much variety in live events (mostly just wrestling and baseball) compared to pre taped. The higher views for live content could be due to less live events but they have higher views, and the taped content could have outlier content that have really high views (or low views) that skewed the data. 

When comparing the mean of top tier live content and mean of top tier taped content, the percent difference is `{r}top_tier_percent_difference` lower views for live content. I interpreted 'top tier' to mean titles that have viewerships higher than average, so I filtered by content that have higher views than the live/taped average (third table). Top tier live content has `{r}top_tier_percent_difference` less views than top tier taped content, which was what I had expected with the previous question, so it's possible outliers skewed the data. A ‘top tier’ live event drew less views that ‘top tier’ pre-taped content.
